newsitem.title: USA: U.S WANTS TO RESTART NUCLEAR REACTOR-LA Times.
newsitem.headline: U.S WANTS TO RESTART NUCLEAR REACTOR-LA Times.

text.p: The Department of Energy wants to restart an ageing nuclear reactor in Hanford, Wash., to produce medical isotopes and tritium, a component of the hydrogen bomb, the Los Angeles Times reported in Monday's editions.

"The department has halted the planned shutdown of Hanford's Fast Flux Test Facility and placed it on 'hot standby' as a prelude to a final decision later this year," the Times said in an article from Hanford.

Saying that the Hanford facility might be the most contaminated place on earth, the newspaper said that by the time it shut down in 1989, it had accumulated 450 billion gallons (1.8 trillion litres) of liquid waste and 200 square miles (517 square km) of contaminated ground water.
The shutdown has been followed by a $2 billion per-year cleanup campaign.

Tritium is a radioactive gas that boosts the explosive power of the hydrogen bomb. According to the Times, the United States has not produced tritium since 1988. The need for tritium now is based on a need to maintain stocks.

The goal of producing radioactive isotopes would be to create jobs by attracting a biopharmaceutical industry, the Times reported. New generation isotopes "are designed to attach themselves to a delivery molecule within the body and attack specific cancer cells, rather than bathing cancer-free tissue in radiation as normal radiation therapy does...."
The treatment has proven to be successful in studies.

Opponents told the newspaper that "restarting the reactor makes no sense when there may be a substantially reduced need for tritium in the future," due to the disarmament process. They also complain about divertimg money from the cleanup and question the potential safety of restarting the reactor.

Supporters include Advanced Nuclear Medical Services, which wants to operate the reactor to make tritium for the government and isotopes for the private sector. The idea that jobs might be produced was welcome in Hanford, where 6,000 jobs have been lost in the last two years, according to the Times.
